title: Design Search Autocomplete
summary: End-to-end walkthrough of typeahead: precomputed top-k per prefix served from memory, a log aggregation pipeline, trending overlays, a per-keystroke latency budget and safety filters.
body:
## Practice first

Design search autocomplete (typeahead) for a large search product: as a user types into the search box, show up to 10 suggested completions for what they have typed so far, ranked by how likely they are to be what the user wants. Suggestions should pick up breaking trends quickly and must never show offensive or legally blocked phrases.

Spend about 10 minutes sketching before reading on: requirements, entities, the one endpoint that matters, a baseline, and how you would hit a latency target on every keystroke. Then compare. This is one defensible design, not the only one.

## Functional requirements

Core (users should be able to):

1. **Get up to 10 suggestions** for the prefix typed so far, ranked mainly by popularity, updated on each keystroke.
2. **See fresh suggestions**: a query that starts trending appears within about 15 minutes; long-term popularity is refreshed daily.
3. **Get safe, lightly personalised suggestions**: blocked terms never appear, and the user's own recent searches can be boosted.

Out of scope: the search results page itself, spelling correction and fuzzy matching (mentioned briefly), voice input, and per-language tokenisation details. We assume one locale per index; other locales get their own index built the same way.

## Non-functional requirements

- **Scale:** 100M daily active searchers, ~1B searches per day, peak ~200,000 suggestion requests per second.
- **Latency:** results must arrive before the next keystroke. People type a character every 150–300 ms, so the target is **p99 under 100 ms end to end**, leaving roughly 10–20 ms for the server.
- **Availability over consistency:** stale suggestions are fine; slow ones are useless. If the service is degraded, return nothing rather than block the search box.
- **Freshness:** trending queries within ~15 minutes, overall ranking within 24 hours.
- **Safety and privacy:** never suggest blocked terms; never surface a rare query that could leak one person's private search (only suggest queries issued by many distinct users).

## Back-of-the-envelope

- **Request rate:** 1B searches/day; with client-side debouncing, assume ~6 suggestion requests per search → 6B/day ≈ 70,000/s average, ~200,000/s peak. Far beyond what a database query per keystroke can serve at 10 ms; this pushes us to **precomputed answers held in memory**.
- **Index size:** keep queries issued by at least, say, 20 distinct users in the window: assume ~100M candidate queries averaging 25 bytes ≈ 2.5 GB of strings. If we precompute the top 10 for each prefix up to 20 characters and only keep prefixes that someone actually types, assume ~300M prefixes × (key ~15 B + 10 × 4-byte query ids + overhead) ≈ 30 GB. That **fits in RAM on one large server**, so we can replicate the whole index rather than shard it. This is the decision that keeps the serving path simple.
- **Replicas:** an in-memory hash lookup plus serialisation handles tens of thousands of requests per second per core-rich host; at ~50k/s per host, 200k/s needs about 4 hosts per region, so 8–10 with headroom and zone redundancy.
- **Log volume:** 1B searches × ~200 bytes of log ≈ 200 GB/day of raw query logs, plus keystroke-level suggestion logs. A daily batch job over this is routine; the trending path must only look at recent minutes.

## Core entities

- **Query log event**: normalised query text, user or session id, timestamp, locale, whether a suggestion was clicked.
- **Query stats**: normalised query → counts over windows (distinct users today, decayed long-term score).
- **Prefix entry**: prefix → ordered list of the top-k query ids with scores. This is the serving index.
- **Blocklist entry**: pattern or exact phrase, reason, added at.
- **User recent queries**: user id → last ~20 queries (for personalisation).

## API

```text
GET /v1/suggest?q=new%20yo&limit=10&locale=en-US
-> 200
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300        (only for unpersonalised responses)
{
  "prefix": "new yo",
  "suggestions": [
    { "text": "new york times", "source": "popular" },
    { "text": "new york weather", "source": "popular" },
    { "text": "new york marathon results", "source": "trending" }
  ]
}

GET /v1/suggest/personal?q=new%20yo     (authenticated, not cacheable)
-> 200 { "suggestions": [ { "text": "new york pizza near me", "source": "history" } ] }
```

The popular endpoint is identical for every user with the same prefix and locale, so it can be cached by browsers and CDNs. Personal suggestions come from a separate, uncacheable call that the client merges, which keeps the shared path cache-friendly. Logging of completed searches happens in the search service, not here.

## High-level design

**Suggestions per keystroke.** The client debounces input, calls `/v1/suggest`, and renders results if they still match the current text. Requests reach a stateless **suggest service** whose hosts each hold the full **prefix index** in memory and answer with a hash lookup.

**Freshness.** An **offline pipeline** turns query logs into the index: logs stream into Kafka, a daily batch job aggregates them into query stats, a builder computes top-k per prefix, filters blocked terms and writes an immutable index file to blob storage. Suggest hosts download new versions and swap atomically. A **streaming job** counts queries over short windows and writes a small **trending overlay** that the service merges in at request time.

**Safety and personalisation.** The builder applies the blocklist; the service also checks a small, fast-updating denylist on every response. Recent searches per user live in a key-value store read by the personal endpoint.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U["Search box"] --> CDN["CDN and edge cache"]
    CDN --> SS["Suggest service, index in RAM"]
    SS --> TR[("Trending overlay")]
    U --> PS["Personal suggest"]
    PS --> RQ[("Recent queries KV")]
    SR["Search service"] --> K[["Query log stream"]]
    K --> BATCH["Daily aggregation"]
    K --> STREAM["Streaming trend counter"]
    BATCH --> BUILD["Index builder and filters"]
    BUILD --> BLOB[("Index snapshots")]
    BLOB --> SS
    STREAM --> TR
```

Walk through a keystroke. The user has typed `new yo`. After a 50 ms pause the client sends the request. The CDN has this prefix cached from another user a minute ago and returns it in 15 ms. For a rarer prefix it would miss, and a suggest host would look up `new yo` in its in-memory map (microseconds), merge any trending entries for that prefix, drop anything on the live denylist, and respond. In parallel the client calls the personal endpoint and puts "new york pizza near me" at the top because the user searched it yesterday.

## Deep dives

### 1. The index data structure (latency)

**Problem:** answer "top 10 completions for this prefix" in well under a millisecond of CPU, for 300M prefixes.

- **Bad: `SELECT ... WHERE query LIKE 'new yo%' ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT 10`.** With a B-tree index the prefix scan is possible, but sorting all matches for a short prefix like `n` means scanning millions of rows per keystroke.
- **Good: a trie, searched at request time.** Walk to the prefix node, then traverse its subtree to find the 10 most popular completions. Prefix lookup is O(length), but the subtree under `n` is enormous, so short prefixes are slow.
- **Great: precompute top-k per prefix.** Store the top 10 at every trie node (or, equivalently and more compactly for serving, a flat hash map from prefix to its top-10 list). A request is one lookup, independent of how many completions exist. The cost moves to build time and memory, both of which we sized above.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    R["root"] --> N["n: new york times, netflix, news"]
    N --> NE["ne: new york times, netflix, news"]
    NE --> NEW["new: new york times, new balance"]
    NEW --> NEWY["new y: new york times, new york weather"]
    NE --> NET["net: netflix, net worth"]
```

Each node stores the prefix's precomputed top completions (shown truncated to two or three), so serving never walks a subtree. The trie view is how the builder computes the lists bottom-up: a node's top-k is the best k of its own terminal query and its children's top-k lists. For serving, the trie can be flattened into a hash map or a compact finite-state transducer, which shares prefixes and suffixes to cut memory further.

Because the whole index fits in RAM we replicate it. If it did not (many locales, much larger vocabularies), shard by a hash of the full prefix rather than by first letter: first-letter ranges create hot shards (`s` and `c` get far more traffic than `x`), whereas each prefix still lives on exactly one shard so no request needs to fan out.

### 2. Building the index from query logs (ranking quality and privacy)

**Problem:** raw logs are noisy. Typos, bots, one user hammering refresh, and private queries ("john smith 42 elm street") must not shape suggestions.

- **Bad: count raw log lines.** One bot or one enthusiastic user dominates; a person's private query appears after they type it twice.
- **Good: normalise and count distinct users.** Lowercase, trim and collapse whitespace, strip punctuation, then count distinct users (or sessions) per query per day. Apply a minimum distinct-user threshold before a query can ever be suggested.
- **Great: decayed scores, quality signals and filters.** Combine daily counts with exponential decay so the score reflects both long-term and recent popularity (`score = Σ count_day × 0.9^age_days`). Boost queries whose suggestions get clicked; demote ones that are typed but abandoned. Remove blocked phrases, adult content for safe-search locales and spam patterns before computing top-k, so a filtered entry frees its slot for the next-best one.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    L[("Raw query logs")] --> N["Normalise and drop bots"]
    N --> D["Count distinct users per day"]
    D --> T["Apply privacy threshold"]
    T --> S["Decayed score and click signals"]
    S --> F["Blocklist and policy filters"]
    F --> K["Top-k per prefix"]
    K --> V["Validate and publish snapshot"]
```

Each stage removes a class of bad suggestion before it can reach the index. The last stage matters operationally: compare the new snapshot with the previous one (size, top prefixes, blocklist hits) and refuse to publish if it differs wildly, because a broken log source can otherwise wipe out suggestions everywhere at once. Snapshots are versioned so a bad one can be rolled back in minutes.

### 3. Trending queries within 15 minutes (freshness)

**Problem:** a daily batch cannot surface "earthquake" ten minutes after one happens.

- **Bad: rebuild the full index every few minutes.** Expensive, and pushing 30 GB to every host that often is wasteful.
- **Good: hourly incremental builds** for prefixes whose stats changed. Helps, but still too slow for breaking events.
- **Great: a small real-time overlay merged at serve time.** A streaming job (Flink, Kafka Streams or similar) counts distinct users per query over sliding 5–15 minute windows, compares with the query's baseline, and flags queries with a sharp rise. For flagged queries it writes `prefix → trending entries` for each of their prefixes into a fast store (or pushes them to suggest hosts). The service merges overlay entries into the base top-k, giving them a bounded number of slots.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Suggest host
    participant B as Base index in RAM
    participant T as Trending overlay
    participant D as Live denylist
    C->>S: suggest q=earthq
    S->>B: lookup earthq
    B-->>S: earthquake proof, earthquake kit
    S->>T: lookup earthq
    T-->>S: earthquake today
    S->>D: filter merged list
    D-->>S: none blocked
    S-->>C: earthquake today first, then base list
```

The base index answers instantly from memory; the overlay lookup is a local or nearby cache read with a strict timeout (if it is slow, return the base list alone). The merged list passes through the live denylist, which is how a legal takedown or an offensive trending phrase is suppressed within minutes rather than at the next daily build. Trending entries carry the same distinct-user threshold so a coordinated bot burst cannot inject a suggestion.

### 4. A latency budget per keystroke (p99 under 100 ms)

| Step | Budget | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Debounce on the client | 0 ms charged (waits for a pause, ~50–100 ms) | Fewer requests; cancel in-flight requests when a new character arrives |
| Network to edge | 20–40 ms | Regional deployment, reused HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection |
| Edge cache hit | ~5 ms | Short prefixes are hot; `max-age` of minutes is fine |
| Suggest host on miss | 5–15 ms | In-memory lookup, no downstream calls except the overlay with a hard timeout |
| Render | under 16 ms | Discard responses that no longer match the input |

Client tricks matter as much as server ones. Cache responses per prefix in the session so backspacing is free. When a list for `new` was the complete set of matches (fewer than 10), the client can filter it locally for `new y` without a request; if it was truncated, it cannot, because the true top 10 for the longer prefix may include items that were not in the shorter list. Ignore out-of-order responses by tagging each request with the text it was for.

### 5. Personalisation and safety (without breaking caching)

Personalising the main response would make every response unique and kill CDN caching. Instead, keep popular suggestions shared and cacheable, and fetch a small personal list (recent searches matching the prefix, from a per-user key-value entry of the last ~20 queries) in parallel; the client merges them, personal first, deduped. Users can clear history, and that deletes the entry. Light contextual signals (country, language) are part of the cache key via the locale parameter rather than per-user state.

Safety is layered: policy filters at build time, the live denylist at serve time, and the distinct-user threshold everywhere. Spelling tolerance, if required, is a separate fuzzy path (edit-distance lookups over a smaller vocabulary) used only when the exact prefix returns few results.

## What interviewers look for

- **Mid-level:** a trie or prefix map, top-k ranking by frequency, a cache, and the separation between the read path and a pipeline that builds the index from logs.
- **Senior:** precomputes top-k per prefix and justifies it with the latency budget, sizes the index to decide between replication and sharding, designs the aggregation (normalisation, distinct users, decay), and adds a trending overlay for freshness.
- **Staff:** treats it as a product with safety and privacy obligations: k-anonymity thresholds, takedown latency, snapshot validation and rollback, multi-locale indexes, client-side behaviour (debounce, cancellation, local filtering rules), and keeping personalisation off the cacheable path.

## Common mistakes

- Querying a database on every keystroke.
- Walking a trie subtree at request time for short prefixes.
- Sharding by first letter and creating hot shards.
- Counting raw log lines, letting bots and single users drive suggestions, or suggesting rare private queries.
- Rebuilding the whole index every few minutes to chase freshness.
- Personalising the shared response and losing edge caching.
- Filtering a truncated list on the client as if it were complete.

## Self-review checklist

- [ ] p99 under 100 ms is broken into a per-step budget, including the client.
- [ ] The serving index holds precomputed top-k per prefix in memory, and its size justifies replication or sharding.
- [ ] The pipeline normalises, counts distinct users, applies a privacy threshold and decays scores.
- [ ] Snapshots are validated, versioned and atomically swapped, with rollback.
- [ ] Trending uses a streaming overlay merged at serve time with a timeout.
- [ ] Blocked terms are filtered at build time and through a live denylist.
- [ ] Personal suggestions are a separate call so shared responses stay cacheable.

keyTakeaways: A per-keystroke budget of about 100 ms leaves 10–20 ms for the server, which rules out database queries and request-time subtree walks.
Precompute the top-k completions for every prefix and serve them from memory; size the index to choose replication over sharding.
Build rankings from logs by normalising, counting distinct users, decaying old counts and enforcing a privacy threshold.
Freshness comes from a small streaming overlay merged at serve time, not from rebuilding the whole index often.
Keep shared suggestions cacheable and fetch personal ones separately; filter unsafe terms at build time and with a live denylist.
